extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and office personnel (and patent practitioners consulting MPEP guidance)
extracted.subtask_description: Examination guidance for determining patent-eligible subject matter (integration of laws/natural principles) and for assessing compliance with the utility requirement (35 U.S.C. 101 and 112, first paragraph). Covers tests (e.g., Mayo/Diehr analysis), making rejections, and evaluating applicant responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of a natural principle into a practical application (Inquiry 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that includes a natural principle must include additional claim features that integrate the principle into a patent-eligible practical application; the additional features must do more than merely recite the natural principle plus routine activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Additional limitations cannot merely limit the field of application (e.g., 'for use in catalytic conversion systems') if that still covers every substantial practical application of the principle. Features that are necessary for all practical applications of the principle (so that everyone practicing the principle must perform them) are insufficient. Use of observable and verifiable steps that show how the principle is employed helps narrow the claim. Examples: Diamond v. Diehr (claims integrating Arrhenius equation with machine and steps were eligible) vs. Mayo (claims reciting correlations plus routine steps were ineligible).

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine-or-transformation showing integration
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciting a particular machine or transformation can demonstrate integration of a natural principle by describing how specific parts implement the principle or how a transformation implements it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A machine that concretely implements the method (e.g., parts of an internal combustion engine) or a transformation that changes the state or thing (not merely position) supports integration. By contrast, a machine or transformation that is merely nominally, insignificantly, or tangentially related (data gathering/storage, incidental apparatus, a computer used only as a weight) does not show integration. Complete absence of such a machine-or-transformation signals a likely disembodied claim directed to a natural principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere statement of a general concept (natural principle) is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that simply state a general concept or law of nature without tangible, specific implementation are directed to the principle itself and are not patent-eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tangible implementations with elements or steps recited with specificity (observable and verifiable steps rather than subjective or imperceptible steps) are required to avoid preemption of the principle. A general instruction to 'apply' the principle or to 'gather data' that merely informs an audience of a law of nature will not suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine/transformation must effect a change beyond mere position/location
rubrics_metrics.description: A recited transformation must involve a change in state or a thing (not merely a change of position or location) to show integration into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transformations that only move an object spatially or recite inconsequential operations are insufficient. The transformation should relate to or implement the natural principle in a way that is substantive and not incidental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making a 35 U.S.C. 101 rejection for claims failing integration (Inquiry 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim fails Inquiry 3 (i.e., does not integrate a natural principle into a patent-eligible practical application), reject under 35 U.S.C. 101 as not drawn to patent-eligible subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A proper rejection should: identify the natural principle; identify that the claim is effectively directed to the natural principle; and explain why the additional claim features or their combination, when considered as a whole, fail to integrate the principle into a practical application or fail to ensure the claim is 'significantly more' than the principle itself. Provide factual reasoning and, where possible, cite supporting authority or evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required content of a sample rejection (analysis & conclusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection should walk through Inquiry 1-3 analysis: whether claim is a statutory category (process/machine/etc.), whether the claim includes a natural principle as a limitation, and whether additional features integrate the principle into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include an explicit analysis showing which Inquiries pass/fail and why (see sample insulin/insulin-testing claim). Conclude with a clear 35 U.S.C. 101 rejection statement and rationale that the claim covers every substantial practical application of the correlation or principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluating and responding to 101 rejections (applicant rebuttal guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proper applicant response may amend claims to add steps/features that integrate the natural principle or provide persuasive arguments/evidence that the additional steps add significantly more than merely describing the principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amendments should practically apply or make use of the principle such that the scope is narrowed beyond the principle plus routine activity. Evidence that the additional steps are not routine, well-known, or conventional can be persuasive (e.g., declarations or publications). Examiner must review amendments, new evidence, and reasoning and recognize/respond to each substantive element of the response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination procedure for utility requirement (general steps)
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel must: read the claims and supporting description; determine what is claimed and any specific embodiments; ensure claims define statutory subject matter (process, machine, manufacture, composition); and determine whether a well-established utility is readily apparent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claimed invention has a well-established utility (one of ordinary skill would immediately appreciate the utility and it is specific, substantial, and credible), do not impose a rejection based on lack of utility. Otherwise, proceed to evaluate asserted utilities for specificity, substantiality, and credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific and substantial utility requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed invention must have a specific and substantial utility — a well-defined, particular benefit to the public, not a general or speculative use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General statements (e.g., 'useful biological properties', 'gene probe' without a target, diagnosing an unspecified disease) are insufficient. An applicant need only provide one credible specific and substantial utility per claimed invention to satisfy the requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credibility of asserted utility (assessment standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Credibility of an asserted utility is assessed from the perspective of a person of ordinary skill in the art in view of the disclosure and any probative evidence of record (test data, declarations, publications, patents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner should accept an applicant's factual statement about utility as true unless countervailing evidence provides legitimate basis to doubt credibility. Expert opinions based on relevant uncontested facts should be accepted; do not reject solely for disagreement over significance or meaning of offered facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to reject for lack of utility and corresponding 35 U.S.C. 112 first paragraph rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: If no asserted specific and substantial credible utility is present and no well-established utility is apparent, reject claims under 35 U.S.C. 101 for lack of utility and under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, for failure to teach how to use the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 35 U.S.C. 101 and 112 rejections shift the burden to the applicant to (i) explicitly identify a specific and substantial utility and (ii) provide evidence that one skilled in the art would have recognized that utility as well-established at filing. Ensure an adequate nexus between submitted evidence and the properties of the claimed subject matter as originally disclosed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima facie showing elements for lack of specific/substantial utility
rubrics_metrics.description: To make a prima facie showing that an asserted utility is not specific/substantial, the examiner must establish it is more likely than not that a person of ordinary skill would not consider the asserted utility specific and substantial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The prima facie showing must include: (i) an explanation setting forth the reasoning for the conclusion, (ii) factual support for findings, and (iii) evaluation of all relevant evidence of record, including utilities taught in the closest prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima facie showing elements for lack of credible utility
rubrics_metrics.description: To make a prima facie showing that an asserted utility is not credible, the examiner must establish it is more likely than not that a person of ordinary skill would not consider any asserted specific and substantial utility credible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The prima facie showing must contain: (i) an explanation of the reasoning concluding the asserted utility is not credible, (ii) support for factual findings relied upon, and (iii) evaluation of all relevant evidence of record (including closest prior art).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner's obligations when making a lack-of-utility rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection based on lack of utility should include detailed explanation and, whenever possible, documentary evidence to support the prima facie showing of no specific/substantial/credible utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide documentary evidence (scientific journals, treatises, patents) or, if unavailable, explain the scientific basis for factual conclusions. If the record does not support the rejection after applicant rebuttal, withdraw the 35 U.S.C. 101 and corresponding 112 rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden shift and applicant rebuttal
rubrics_metrics.description: Once examiner makes a proper prima facie showing of lack of specific/substantial/credible utility, the burden shifts to the applicant to rebut by amending claims, providing reasoning, or submitting evidence (declarations, patents, printed publications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must review original disclosure, prior evidence, claim amendments, and any new reasoning or evidence submitted. Only maintain the rejection if the totality of the record continues to show lack of specific, substantial, and credible utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and examples of 'specific utility'
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific utility provides a well-defined and particular benefit to the public, tied to the claimed subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of insufficient specificity: claiming a compound 'useful in treating unspecified disorders' or ESTs described only as general 'gene probes' without target. Contrast with disclosing a specific biological activity reasonably correlated to a disease condition — that may be sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and examples of 'substantial utility'
rubrics_metrics.description: Substantial utility denotes an immediate, well-defined, real-world benefit to the public; utilities that require further research to identify or confirm a real-world context are not substantial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of non-substantial utilities: (A) basic research on properties, (B) methods for treating unspecified diseases, (C) assays identifying materials that themselves lack specific/substantial utility, (D) methods of making a material that has no specific/substantial/credible utility, (E) claims to intermediate products used to make a final product that lacks specific/substantial utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research tools and intermediate products — not per se excluded from utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventions used in research settings (research tools, assays, instruments) can have specific and substantial utility if their disclosed use provides an immediate benefit; labels like 'research tool' are not determinative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish inventions that identify a specific substantial utility in current form from those whose asserted utility requires further research. Examiner should focus on whether a claimed invention has a specific and substantial utility, not on the setting in which it will be used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wholly inoperative/incredible utility standard
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention is only unpatentable for lack of utility if it is totally incapable of producing any useful result; a small degree of utility is sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejecting for inoperability or 'incredible' utility requires proof of total incapacity. Partial success or imperfect performance does not justify a lack-of-utility rejection. Courts require total incapacity before sustaining a 35 U.S.C. 101 denial on these grounds.
